input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Detail the evidence retrieval protocol per section (query formation and scope), ranking/scoring criteria for candidate snippets, and the mechanism for selecting and injecting evidence into generation prompts. Also cover evidence provenance tracking and minimal formatting requirements for injected items.

output:
This section specifies the protocol used to retrieve, rank, and inject evidence for the generation of individual sections. The protocol is presented as a reproducible sequence of operations that (a) forms section-targeted retrieval queries, (b) defines a lightweight scoring and ranking procedure for candidate snippets, (c) selects a small set of high-confidence items for prompt injection, and (d) records provenance and minimal formatting metadata for every injected item. All factual assertions produced by downstream generators are required, by design, to reference one or more injected evidence items; the workflow therefore privileges conservative selection and explicit provenance over broad, noisy recall.

Query formation and retrieval scope. For each section node we construct a focused retrieval query intended to capture the section's information need. The query combines: (i) the section title and any author-provided seed notes, (ii) the immediate predecessor node summaries in the document graph when available (to preserve local dependency context), and (iii) a short set of task constraints (e.g., ``definitions only'', ``empirical results'', or ``related work citations''). The retrieval scope is limited to a user-specified corpus (for our experiments, internal notes and a curated PDF set where available) and to document segments that conform to a minimal snippet length. This scoped retrieval reduces both topical drift and the risk of injecting distant, low-relevance evidence.

Candidate scoring and ranking. Retrieved candidates are represented as short snippets with attached metadata (document id, location, and surrounding sentence context). We compute an internal relevance score for each candidate using a configurable similarity metric between the section query and candidate representation (for example, lexical overlap combined with embedding similarity). Candidates are then ranked by descending relevance score. In keeping with the system's conservative design, we retain only the top-ranked candidates that meet simple acceptability checks (presence of an explicit bibliographic identifier, extractability of a concise quote or paraphrase, and absence of obvious OCR or parsing errors).

Selection and injection policy. From the ranked list we select a compact set of evidence items to inject into the generation prompt. The injected set is chosen to balance three objectives: topical coverage of the section subtopics, redundancy avoidance (do not inject multiple near-duplicate snippets), and provenance completeness (each injected item must include a document identifier). The injection into the prompt follows a deterministic template: each item is presented with a short label, the quoted snippet or paraphrase, and a provenance line. The generator is explicitly instructed to (1) cite the corresponding provenance label when making factual claims derived from the item and (2) avoid inventing facts not grounded in an injected item. Prompts include a JSON schema fragment that enumerates required fields for every asserted fact (fact text, supporting item id(s), and statement confidence), thereby coupling generation to downstream validation.

Provenance tracking and minimal formatting. For every injected evidence item the system records the following minimal metadata fields: source_id, source_type (e.g., internal_note or pdf), page_or_location, snippet_text, extracted_sentence_context, and extraction_method (quote or paraphrase). These fields are emitted alongside the generated section in the JSON-constrained output so that assembly into LaTeX and refs.bib can reliably reconstruct citations and allow auditors to inspect the exact supporting text. The snippet_text is kept short (single sentence when possible) and is stored in raw plain text to avoid LaTeX-escaping issues during later assembly.

Validation checks and failure handling. Prior to finalizing the injected set, the pipeline applies conservative validation checks: every candidate must have non-empty source_id metadata, snippet_text must pass a minimal tokenization sanity check, and overlapping snippets from the same location are collapsed to a single representative item. If no candidate satisfies these checks for a given section, the pipeline will (a) fallback to emitting a structural placeholder in the JSON output that flags the section as evidence-missing, and (b) avoid producing unsupported factual claims for that section. These failure modes are surfaced explicitly in the JSON output to facilitate human intervention or iterative retrieval refinement.

Implementation notes and auditability. The protocol is intentionally modular: the retrieval back end, similarity metric, and acceptability checks can be replaced independently while preserving the injection and provenance schema. All injected items and their metadata are retained in machine-readable form to support automated audits (e.g., coverage checks that compare the set of asserted facts against supporting item ids) and manual review. Because no external citations are implicitly invented by the generator, post-hoc edits and corrections are straightforward: auditors can add, remove, or replace injected items and then re-run section generation with the updated evidence set.

Limitations. The above protocol emphasizes conservative evidence use and explicit provenance tracking; however, its effectiveness depends on the quality and coverage of the underlying retrieval corpus and on the chosen similarity metric. When the retrieval corpus lacks relevant materials, the system will produce evidence-missing placeholders rather than unsupported assertions, which preserves conservatism but may increase manual workload. These trade-offs are considered in the experimental evaluation and in the Discussion.
